S001.name: Detail_Inattention_Errors
S001.description: Often fails to give close attention to details or makes careless mistakes.
examples: Makes mistakes in homework or tests by misreading questions or skipping important parts.
Frequently omits details or makes typos in work documents or reports.
Repeats mistakes in calculations or numerical work, such as switching signs or getting digits wrong.
Performs tasks incorrectly by missing important details in instructions.

S003.name: Listening_Difficulty
S003.description: Often does not seem to listen when spoken to directly.
examples: Appears not to be listening, looking elsewhere or spacing out during conversation.
Immediately asks to repeat what was just said or instructed.
Does not respond when name is called or answers only after a long delay.
Misses the content of the conversation, giving unrelated answers or out-of-context reactions.

S010.name: Fidgeting
S010.description: Often fidgets with or taps hands or feet or squirms in seat.
examples: Constantly shaking legs or twisting and squirming body while seated.
Spinning a pen or fiddling with nearby objects, unable to keep hands still.
Continually changing posture and feeling uncomfortable while sitting.
Constantly moving, such as tapping the desk with fingers or tapping feet on the floor.

S011.name: Leaving_Seat
S011.description: Often leaves seat in situations when remaining seated is expected.
examples: Frequently leaves seat or wanders around during class or meetings using excuses.
Unable to sit still during meals and keeps getting up.
Leaves seat in the middle of a movie or performance to go to the restroom or go outside.
Continually leaves seat and wanders around in the office where one is expected to sit and work.

S012.name: Feeling_Restless
S012.description: Often runs about or climbs in situations where it is inappropriate. (Note: In adolescents or adults, may be limited to feeling restless.)
examples: Feels uncomfortable and restless as if something is squirming inside when sitting still.
Feels internally anxious and stifled in situations requiring prolonged sitting.
A sense of urgency and anxiety that one must keep moving or doing something.
Feels unable to endure staying still and must constantly be doing something.

S014.name: Constant_Activity
S014.description: Is often 'on the go', acting as if 'driven by a motor'.
examples: Constantly moving and active as if driven by a motor.
Starts another task immediately after finishing one, without resting for a moment.
Unable to stay still even on weekends or days off, constantly doing something.
Appears to others to be always busy and bustling about.

S016.name: Blurting_Answers
S016.description: Often blurts out an answer before a question has been completed.
examples: Raises hand or blurts out the answer before the question is even finished in class or meetings.
Jumps to conclusions and speaks before the other person finishes their sentence.
Answers hastily without reading the question to the end in quizzes or exams.
Interrupts and answers in the middle of a conversation without listening to the other person until the end.

S018.name: Interrupting_Intruding
S018.description: Often interrupts or intrudes on others (e.g., butts into conversations, games, or activities).
examples: Butts into conversations of others where they have not been invited.
Joins in on others' work or games without permission or interferes.
Touches or uses other people's belongings or work without permission.
Keeps talking to and disturbing others when they are focusing on work or studying.

symptom.disease_info: Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder, Predominantly Hyperactive/Impulsive Presentation, is characterized by developmentally inappropriate levels of motor activity, restlessness, impulsive actions, and difficulty waiting or inhibiting responses, with comparatively fewer or less prominent inattentive symptoms. In adults, it often presents as inner restlessness, difficulty staying seated, a sense of being "driven," and impulsive decision-making that impairs work, relationships, or safety. Symptoms must be longstanding, begin in childhood, and be present across settings, but many adults only recognize the pattern when job demands, parenting, or complex multitasking exceed their compensatory routines. It must be differentiated from anxiety, bipolar spectrum conditions, substance use, and personality traits by the pervasiveness, early onset, and specific pattern of hyperactive/impulsive behaviors across contexts.

patient.stressor: Over the past two years, Vilma’s role gradually shifted from mostly controlled, solo camera work and editing to more complex shoots where she had to sit through long production meetings, coordinate with larger crews, and juggle multiple projects in post-production. As deadlines stacked up and responsibilities expanded, she found it increasingly difficult to tolerate the long, static stretches of planning and client reviews that her hoped-for move into a senior director of photography role required, despite her otherwise meticulous, routine-driven personality. This mismatch between her need for constant movement and the industry’s expectation that she remain in her seat for hours during table reads, color sessions, and festival panels led to subtle conflict with collaborators, missed networking opportunities at festivals, and self-doubt about whether she could handle leadership. After a producer she respected gently commented that her inability to stay put in meetings was becoming distracting and might limit her promotion prospects, she sought psychiatric evaluation to understand why she could not seem to remain seated even in situations that mattered deeply to her career.
patient.chief_complaint: “I can’t sit through long production meetings or edit sessions anymore—I keep getting up and pacing even when I know I should stay in my seat.”

patient.stressor: For years, Hakim’s high-energy style on the production floor was seen as an asset, but about two years ago his company increased line speeds and introduced stricter quality and safety protocols tied directly to performance bonuses. At the same time, his impulsive spending on travel, vinyl, and gear began to strain the family budget, making those bonuses and steady overtime crucial to keeping up with bills and a modest savings plan he and his spouse had agreed upon. Under this pressure, he noticed that his tendency to jump ahead in conversations, make snap decisions, and cut corners to "move things along" at work was leading to more documented errors, safety write-ups, and tension with supervisors, which in turn threatened his income and caused frequent money arguments at home. After nearly losing a quarterly bonus due to a series of impulsive mistakes that jeopardized his push for CNC certification, and his spouse pointing out a pattern of him talking over people and derailing important financial discussions, he agreed to see a psychiatrist to figure out why he keeps interrupting and acting before thinking, even when he knows the consequences hit their wallet directly.
patient.chief_complaint: “I keep cutting people off and jumping into things before they’re finished talking or deciding, and it’s starting to mess up my job and my money.”

patient.stressor: Around two years ago, Isabella’s company underwent a major restructuring that elevated her from a mostly individual contributor role into leading cross-functional sourcing teams and sitting through extended vendor negotiations, budget reviews, and KPI presentations. This transition required her to remain engaged for long, back-to-back meetings and to listen closely as colleagues and suppliers presented detailed information, a sharp contrast to the more dynamic, project-based work and quiet analysis she had previously organized around her own rhythms. She began to notice that during these long sessions, her mind would drift despite her competitive, disciplined nature, leading to missed details that affected purchasing decisions and forced her to stay late correcting issues, which cut into her solitary evenings of yoga, painting, and reading. After a high-stakes contract review where she realized she had completely tuned out a key section and had to be corrected by a junior analyst, she felt embarrassed and worried that something was fundamentally wrong with how she processed information in group settings, prompting her to seek psychiatric assessment.
patient.chief_complaint: “In long meetings, people talk directly to me and I just zone out—I realize afterward I didn’t really hear what they were saying.”
